chapters.title: Capability domains
chapters.heading: Five lenses on every deployment
chapters.lede: Cyber, data, digital, technology, and the legal-ethical frame around them. Each domain has its own authoritative guidance; a deployment is ready only when all five say so. That is why the team is multidisciplinary.

kids.v: NCSC Guidelines for secure AI system development cover secure design, development, deployment and operation. Agreed with CISA and 21 international agencies; aimed at any system that uses AI, built or bought.

Secure by Design and the Government Cyber Security Standard apply to AI services like any other, plus AI-specific threat modelling: prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction, over-permissioned agents.
NCSC's principles for the security of machine learning translate the threats into controls. Walk before you run with agentic AI.
The Data Ethics Framework guides appropriate, responsible data use across the public sector: transparency, accountability, fairness.

UK GDPR and the DPA 2018 require a DPIA before high-risk processing. The ICO's AI guidance, with a statutory AI code of practice in development, is the regulator's view of what good looks like. Cross-border processing (for example a US-processed model behind a UK product) needs a Transfer Risk Assessment as well as SCCs.
The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard is mandatory for central departments and arms-length bodies: a published record for every in-scope algorithmic tool.

Model quality is data quality: govern provenance, representativeness and retention for training and grounding data alike — retrieval systems inherit the permissions, quality and currency of the estate.
AI Playbook for the UK Government
The Service Standard and Service Manual set the operating model: start with user needs, work in multidisciplinary teams, iterate in the open. AI services are still services.
The AI Playbook and the AI Knowledge Hub supply the patterns, case studies and communities; the PM's AI Exemplars programme is the test-and-learn engine for scaling what works.
Accessibility is law, not polish: WCAG 2.2 AA under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018. AI interfaces (chat, voice, summaries) need their own accessibility evidence.
The Technology Code of Practice governs the technology choices: cloud first, interoperability, open standards, sustainability, exit.
Compute and infrastructure are national policy: AI Growth Zones and a compute roadmap from 21 ExaFLOPs (2025) towards 420 by 2030 under the AI Opportunities Action Plan.
Buy well: use Crown Commercial Service AI routes, insist on evaluation access and model-change notice in contracts, and design the exit before signing the entry.

The Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty apply to automated and AI-assisted decisions. Public-law duties (fairness, rationality, giving reasons) still bind when a model is in the loop.

Explainability has a manual: 'Explaining decisions made with AI', by the ICO and The Alan Turing Institute — and explanations shown to people should reference functional needs, never a diagnosis or label.
Public trust is earned in the open: engage affected people early, say clearly where AI is used, and give a route to challenge and redress.

chapters.heading: Principles with tests, gates with teeth
chapters.lede: A three-tier canon governs everything that influences how something is built — prototypes explicitly included, because most principle breaches enter the estate through prototypes that were never intended to survive, and then did.

body.v: Tier 1 conformance is binary: the principle applies and is met, or a recorded exception exists. No informal partial conformance.
Tier 2 — the core seven, each with a test

items.v: **Test:** Can each element be traced to a named authoritative owner outside the central platform?**Looks compliant, is not:** "We will federate later, once everything is in one place."
**Test:** Can a user discover an asset exists without thereby gaining access to it?**Looks compliant, is not:** Endpoint or credential details published as discovery metadata for convenience.
**Test:** Can any automated component write to the record without recorded human approval?**Looks compliant, is not:** "The user can always review it" — optional review presented as a control.
**Test:** Take any output at random: can you reconstruct inputs, owner, decision and evidence without asking a person?**Looks compliant, is not:** Evidence linked at closure rather than at capture.
**Test:** Is there a recorded reuse assessment that predates the build decision?**Looks compliant, is not:** Reuse assessment performed after the build decision, to justify it.

**Test:** Is accessibility evidence produced before release? Does every status carry a non-colour cue?**Looks compliant, is not:** "We will run an accessibility audit before go-live" as the only accessibility activity.
**Test:** Attempt to breach the control through the normal interface. Does it succeed?**Looks compliant, is not:** A mandatory gate with no exception path — guaranteeing informal workarounds.

body.v: **Prototype promotion gate.** A prototype may not be promoted toward live use until Tier 1 and Tier 2 conformance is assessed and recorded. Record intended lifespan and disposal point at creation; record deferred principles; re-assess them at the gate. Human-in-the-loop applies in full even at prototype stage — autonomy introduced early is rarely removed later. Promotion is a decision, not a drift.

kids.v: From the AI Engineering Lab's reference implementation: the transferable innovation is not any one use case — it is the operating model around it. Specialist agents routed by an orchestrator; a challenger agent that reviews outputs; a compliance agent; assurance gates executed in the workflow; immutable audit trails; human approval before anything writes to the record. The same pattern serves capability management, catalogue operations, workforce planning and architecture governance.

A gate, not a form: run at the end of every iteration. Tier 0 is the brake — the only tier that can argue for less; a veto is the instrument doing its job. chapters.title: Human oversight principles
chapters.heading: The human directs; AI is in the loop
chapters.lede: Ten principles for keeping people in charge of AI-assisted work: oversight is a competence to build and measure, not a box to tick. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: **Proposed** items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

kids.v: P1 The human directs; AI is in the loop

The person is always in the director position. AI works inside a scope the person sets, and is given agency only if, when and where it is warranted. Oversight competence means setting good bounds, reading the evidence that they are wrong, and withdrawing agency without the service collapsing.

Classify every deployment as assist, recommend or determine before choosing controls. The productivity evidence comes from drafting, summarising and analysis; none of it comes from determining anything about a person. Drafting-grade controls on determination is the real risk; determination-grade controls on drafting forfeits real value.
P3 Attention is a budget, not a tax

Most interactions should carry no friction. High-consequence, high-uncertainty and novel cases get the full set. The first control is to reduce what reaches a person at all: triage, confidence-gating and risk-proportionate friction. You cannot train your way out of a capacity problem.
P4 Measure oversight; never assume it

Every UK instrument makes human oversight the primary safeguard and none checks whether it still works. Behavioural signals lead; self-report, attestation and training completion do not count as evidence.
P5 Measure the system, never the person

Oversight measurement is aggregate and non-attributable, enforced in code with minimum cohort sizes. Individual-level oversight measurement is ruled out in any form. Unions are design partners before build, on a just-culture basis.

Evidence of maintained oversight is what lets a team take the human out of more loops safely. Positioned as a brake it will be routed around; positioned as the route to more autonomy, delivery teams will ask for it.

No figure, citation, claim or capability is asserted unless it can be reproduced from a source or the data. What cannot be reproduced is labelled modelled, estimated or unconfirmed on the face of the artefact. Treat any AI-produced draft as hypotheses.

Using AI to get past a stable barrier (structuring a draft, checking tone, holding many things in mind) is assistive technology. Using it to replace a judgement you could form yourself is where skill atrophy lives. A blanket rule to keep using skills unaided would be an accessibility regression.
P9 Disclose AI assistance at the right level

Classify AI-assisted work by audience (internal, peer co-design, external) and apply the matching disclosure. The human keeps the framework, structure, final selection and original contributions; AI output is raw material that is reviewed, accepted, rejected and shaped.
P10 Evidence-led, with a stated exit

If longitudinal research finds no material oversight decay in administrative settings, the currency regime scales back to sampling only. Stating in advance what would change our mind is what keeps the programme evidence-led.

chapters.heading: Controls that keep oversight real
chapters.lede: 30 controls, each placed by who applies it (layer), what it does (prevent, detect, recover) and the lowest class of deployment it applies to: assist, recommend or determine. rows.v: Record the reviewer's provisional judgement before the machine output is shown. Prevents anchoring, generates a continuous unaided baseline as a by-product of normal work, and sidesteps the industrial-relations problem because it is a workflow feature rather than an assessment. At director level the same pattern applies upstream: state in advance what you expect the agent to produce and what would cause you to withdraw its grant.
Withhold the recommendation where model uncertainty is highest, concentrating independent reasoning exactly where the machine is least reliable.
Surface what contradicts the recommendation, not what justifies it. Explanations alone do not reduce overreliance and may increase it.
Approval requires a reason, not a button. Mild forcing function, quality signal, and the audit trail that makes decisions defensible.
After a run of unmodified approvals the interface changes state. Rubber-stamping has a behavioural signature and can be interrupted where it appears.
Unmistakable, persistent visual distinction between an agent proposing and an agent acting, with a plain-language capability statement shown every time.
Distinguish retrieved fact, computed value and generated inference within one output. Reviewers apply different scrutiny to each and currently cannot tell them apart.
An explicit work-without-the-agent mode as a first-class path. If the unaided path is slow or missing, unaided practice will not happen whatever the policy says.
Explanation mode by default in unfamiliar or security-critical code; generation mode where the developer already holds the model. Usage pattern matters more than the tool.
Before merge, the author answers a generated question about their own diff. Targets comprehension debt where it is created rather than where it causes an incident.
Keep incident response and root-cause work assistant-free by default. Debugging degrades most and is exactly what validates everything else.
Throughput rising while time-in-review per change falls is the signature of oversight collapse, and looks like a productivity win on standard metrics.
Truck-factor and ownership metrics assume the committer understands the code. Once much of it is machine-generated, organisations believe they have knowledge coverage they do not have.
Tests for agent-generated code should not come from the same agent in the same pass, or verification and artefact share a failure mode.
One event per interaction, comparable across the estate. Building this per-department guarantees incomparable data and no exportable artefact.
Minimum cohort sizes enforced in code, so individual analysis is structurally unavailable rather than merely prohibited. Far more credible to staff than a policy promise.
Synthetic known-bad outputs at low randomised rate with guaranteed downstream suppression. The sharpest instrument available and the fastest way to lose the programme if sequenced wrong.
Human trust calibration is built against a specific error profile. A silent upgrade resets it and every reviewer's intuition is tuned to a system that no longer exists.
Records last unaided practice, canary exposure and comprehension check — by role, never by person.
Deployment plans must state the oversight burden, who carries it, the headcount cost and how approval fatigue is mitigated as volume scales.
Named owner with delegate; pause, reassign or deactivate on offboarding; explicit transfer of accountability or the agent stops.
Periodically demonstrate the service runs without the agent at acceptable quality. A continuity exercise, not a workforce assessment — which also avoids the industrial-relations problem.
Attention is a budget. Most interactions get none; high-consequence, high-uncertainty, novel cases get the full set. The system should read as removing friction from routine work.

Agency is granted, not assumed. Teams that show sustained catch performance and good outcome sampling earn lighter per-item oversight and wider agent scope. Every grant states, before it is issued, what the director expects the agent to produce, what evidence would trigger withdrawal, and a costed path to withdraw it without the service collapsing (the degraded-mode standard).
Rebuild entry-level roles around verification, evaluation and supervised judgement. The longest-lead item here, and the only risk no other control addresses.
Require draft-only defaults, immutable logging, explainable action chains, declared autonomy level, and evidence that the approval interface does not induce rubber-stamping.
A reusable component that captures the human's provisional judgement before revealing the agent's output. this is the highest-value single primitive.
A test harness verifying that a product implements P1–P6 correctly. Built on Inspect, this doubles as the procurement conformance test and the exportable artefact.

Unaided debugging and design reasoning remain part of promotion and hiring assessment. If the profession stops selecting for it, no downstream control will preserve it.

items: **Treat an AI-produced research draft as hypotheses only.** An AI-produced research draft was treated as a source of hypotheses only. None of its assertions was carried forward unchecked. **Keep unverifiable claims, marked.** Claims that could not be substantiated were kept and marked. Deleting them would remove the evidence of the checking.

**Provenance travels with each claim.** The unit here is the claim, not the document. In a portal people land on one assertion without meeting the caveats that make it safe to use, so the provenance travels with each claim.

items: Is a DPIA required? Probably yes at tier 2 and certainly at tier 3. The processing concerns staff conduct at work, involves systematic monitoring of a workforce, and relates to the evaluation of performance — even though the design deliberately prevents individual evaluation. Argue it through rather than assuming the aggregation exempts you.

The question your DPO will ask: if it is genuinely non-identifying, why does it need a DPIA? Answer: because the collection point is identifying, and because the risk being assessed is function creep, not the current design.

kids.v: Equality impact assessment — the questions that actually bite

items: The generic template will not surface the real issues. These will.

Differential effect of friction. Cognitive forcing interventions benefit people with higher need for cognition more than others. Uniform application therefore produces unequal benefit. Who is disadvantaged — staff with dyslexia, ADHD, English as an additional language, high caseloads, caring responsibilities affecting available concentration?

Reasonable adjustments. Does predict-then-reveal interact badly with any assistive technology in use? Has it been tested with a screen reader, with magnification, and at the time pressure a real queue applies?

Cohort composition. If cohorts map to teams, and teams differ systematically in composition, aggregate comparison between cohorts can become proxy discrimination. Check before publishing cohort comparisons.
Who is in determine-class roles? If the roles carrying the heaviest oversight burden are disproportionately held by any group, the burden is not equally distributed.

Effect of the junior-role finding. If entry-level roles are being reshaped, who currently holds them and who is affected by their redesign? This has a clear equality dimension and is the longest-lead item in the programme.
Language. Where the body has Welsh Language Standards obligations, the interface and any staff-facing materials fall within them.
Do not conclude "no impact". The honest finding is that the impact is real, differential and manageable — and that uniform friction is the version that fails the duty.

kids.v: Trade union engagement — a note to open the conversation

items: Draft for adaptation. Send before anything is built, not before it launches.
We are proposing to measure whether human oversight of AI systems in this service is working. We want to design it with you, and there is one design decision we would rather you set than we did.

The background: every instrument governing our use of AI treats human oversight as the main safeguard. None of them checks whether that safeguard is functioning. That is a risk to the public and, more immediately, a risk to members — because a colleague placed in an approval loop without the time, information or practised skill to exercise it meaningfully is not exercising accountability. They are absorbing liability for an institutional decision they could not realistically have controlled.
What we are proposing to measure: how the service as a whole is performing — how quickly outputs are approved, how much they are changed, whether errors are being caught.

What we are not proposing to measure, in any form: individual performance. There is no user identifier in the data schema. The schema is closed, so one cannot be added. The analysis tools refuse any query resolving to fewer than ten people, and refuse outright any file containing an identifier column. This is enforced in code rather than promised in policy, because we think a promise is worth less than a system that cannot do the thing.

What we would like to agree with you before we build: that this operates on a just-culture basis — closer to confidential safety reporting in aviation than to appraisal; that findings are never attributed, formally or informally; that participation in any unaided practice or sampling is scheduled work rather than an addition to workload; and that we jointly review, annually, whether any request for individual-level data has been made, and record that it was refused.
What we would ask in return: that where the measurement shows oversight is not working, the response is to fix the workload, the interface or the deployment — not the individual.
We would rather have this conversation now, at design stage, than present you with something finished. If the answer is that this cannot be made acceptable, we would rather know before we build it.

kids.v: Ethics application for canary injection — the content that will be asked for

items: Only needed at tier 3. Expect months, not weeks.
What is proposed. Injecting synthetic known-bad AI outputs, at a low randomised rate, into a live review queue, to measure whether reviewers detect them.

Why it cannot be done in a simulation. Detection under real time pressure, real caseload and real fatigue is the thing being measured. A laboratory version measures something else. This is the same reasoning behind live fire drills and phishing simulations, both of which have established precedent in government.

Harm to the public — the safety case. No canary can reach a citizen. Injected items are suppressed downstream by the platform regardless of the reviewer's disposition. State the technical mechanism, not the intention. Include the failure mode: what happens if the suppression fails, how it would be detected, and how quickly.

Harm to staff. Reviewers know canaries exist but not which items they are. The measure is aggregate and non-attributable; failing to catch one has no individual consequence and cannot be traced to a person. Address the stress question directly: this is a workload and design intervention if catch rates fall, not a disciplinary one.

Consent. Individual consent is not sought, for the same reason it is not sought for fire drills — announced tests measure announced behaviour. Collective agreement is sought instead, through the recognised unions, and staff are told the programme exists, its purpose, and that results are never individual.
Withdrawal. The union side can suspend injection. Say so explicitly; it is what makes the collective-agreement route legitimate.
Data. Canary events carry no identifier. Retention as per the DPIA.
Reporting. Aggregate catch rate by canary class, reported to the service owner and the SRO. Published internally including when results are poor.

The question the committee will ask: what happens if catch rates are very low? Answer in advance: it triggers a review of workload, interface and deployment scope — and, for a determine-class service, consideration of whether the deployment should continue in its current form. If you cannot commit to that, the case for injecting is weak.

chapters.title: Neuroinclusive AI at work

chapters.lede: How AI tools help and hinder people across neurotypes at work, how to talk about them without a deficit framing, and the questions that are still open. Build one version that works for everyone, layered, rather than a separate one. From the Responsible AI and Data Use (RAIDU) work, merged into this playbook on 22 November 2026. Each item keeps its evidence grade: **Proposed** items are design proposals for review, not policy or established practice.

items: **Don't build two versions (one for neurodiverse staff, one for everyone else)**. Managers' attitudes shaped use and control-group awareness was low; a split communication badges it as a 'special accommodation', undersells it to neurotypical staff and stigmatises it for neurodiverse staff.
**Lead with the curb-cut framing, not the deficit framing**. Outcome language ('levelled the playing field'), not diagnosis language. Avoid 'crutch' language even to knock it down.
**Layer the detail rather than write two documents: a one-page plain-language summary with the fuller evidence base undern** eath.

**Talking to your manager: frame it in terms of outcome, not diagnosis ('this helps me structure written work faster and m** ore confidently'); no need to disclose a condition; if it functions as a genuine accessibility aid, say so explicitly so it is treated like any reasonable adjustment if the licence is reviewed.
**For managers: neutral, informed encouragement - not enthusiasm or scepticism - produces the best outcomes for the whole** team.

**one layout/format alone will not meet everyone's needs (some autism sub-types are polar oppos** ites); present tailored around common characteristics or a compromise that best serves all; Easy Read version is a must. This partly overrides the turn-5 'one layered document' advice: the turn-11 solution is a characteristics poster plus a separate Easy Read version.
**Don't blanket-licence**. Target by task profile first, need second (admin-heavy/high-information roles benefited; Legal and Policy did not).
**Fund self-led exploration over formal training sessions; budget time, not just courseware (p < 0**.01 at 2+ hours self-led use).

**Plan continuity, not just onboarding**. If a licence functions as assistive technology for someone, treat withdrawal with the same seriousness as withdrawing any other reasonable adjustment, not as an IT asset reclaim.

**Build QA expectations that vary by task, not a blanket 'always check' policy nobody follows**. Drafting/summarising: light-touch spot-check. Data analysis and anything feeding a decision: mandate verification (DBT observed tasks showed Copilot users did worse on Excel analysis).
**Track dependency alongside satisfaction in any evaluation commissioned; none of the three government evaluations measure** d these jointly at individual level - a genuine gap.
**Cost transparency matters to uptake: address ethical/environmental concerns rather than dismiss them**.

**Model-dependent findings** Describe a specific model's failure mode at a specific point in time (e.g. 2024 ChatGPT advising an autistic user to 'just walk up and start talking'). Testable claims, not settled facts. Re-run the equivalent prompt against current models before relying on it (five-minute check). Tag [model-dependent — re-verify before citing]; note model and test date; anything older than about six months needs a fresh spot-check.
**Structural (human-factors and organisational) findings** About people and institutions, not the model. Safe to build governance policy on now. Tag [structural — durable].

**More fluent models are more persuasive when wrong** Newer, more fluent, more agreeable models are not guaranteed to reduce dependency risk — they may increase it, because a model better at sounding authoritative and more consistently agreeable is more persuasive when wrong. 'The tooling has evolved' is a reason to scrutinise sycophancy and over-reliance harder, not to trust more.

**Is chatbot-based support for autistic people legitimate assistive technology, or a paternalistic fix aimed at the wrong target?** For: Autistic users in the CMU study chose this themselves, unprompted by clinicians, because existing workplace support was inadequate or absent — 'it's the only thing I trust.' Respecting autonomy means respecting that choice, not gatekeeping it behind professional approval. Against: A review Begel co-authored found 90% of HRI research on autism excluded autistic perspectives — a documented history of building 'solutions' nobody with autism wanted. Chatbot advice-giving individualises a structural workplace-inclusion failure: asking an autistic employee to get better at masking via AI coaching instead of making the workplace accessible treats the symptom.

**Does satisfaction without measured productivity gain justify public licensing spend?** For: DBT frames wellbeing, confidence and inclusion as legitimate outcomes independent of output volume; a more sustainable, less anxious workforce is a defensible use of public money, especially for a protected characteristic. Against: DBT's own conclusion: no evidence time savings led to improved productivity; value for money unassessed. Licences justified by self-reported satisfaction are weak in any Treasury-facing review and risk being read as subsidised comfort.

**Does normalising AI-mediated compensation reduce institutional pressure to provide genuine accommodation?** For: (risk is real) If AI drafting becomes the default fix for a dyslexic employee, the organisation has less incentive to fund proper adjustments, job redesign or human support - AI is cheaper and needs no line-management change. Against: Assumes accommodation is zero-sum; DBT and Capita evidence shows the tool works alongside existing adjustments and often surfaces previously invisible/unfunded need - additive, not replacement.

**Universal rollout versus targeted, disclosure-based provisioning?** For: (universal) Curb-cut argument: benefits accrue to non-native English speakers, hearing- and vision-impaired staff and many neurotypical staff (80% of use cases rated satisfactory across DBT). Targeting requires disclosure, which carries stigma risk (CMU respondents worried). Against: Untargeted rollout produced DBT's finding that Legal and Policy roles got minor benefit while absorbing the same licence cost and verification burden; also removes a comparison group, making it harder to tell real accessibility benefit from placebo/novelty.

**Is self-report evidence trustworthy?** For: Confidence, cognitive load and satisfaction are inherently subjective - self-report is the correct instrument. DBT triangulated with interviews and observed tasks and found broadly consistent patterns. Against: Respondents volunteered (70% of DBT) or knew they were evaluated on a tool their employer promoted - social-desirability and novelty bias. The only non-self-report measure (observed tasks) contradicted diary data on Excel analysis and PowerPoint quality.

**Is it responsible to act on this evidence at all, given how fast tooling changes?** For: (act now) Waiting for model-current research means never acting. Structural findings (manager influence, training modality, compensatory-vs-substitutive risk) are durable - acting on those is low-risk. Against: The most policy-relevant claims (advice quality, hallucination frequency, persuasiveness/over-reliance risk) are model-dependent and most likely wrong by the time a document reaches a minister. Citing a 2024 finding as current without re-testing is a factual risk.

chapters.title: Pace & parity
chapters.heading: Named once. Controlled nowhere.
chapters.lede: Skill atrophy appears in this guide as a single sentence in the evidence chapter, credited to Canada. Nothing sits behind it: no control, no metric, no register field, no gate criterion, no owner. That is the honest answer to the question, and it is now backlog item **PACE-01**. This chapter closes it, then applies the same test to everything else the world has built that we have not.

kids.v: One sentence, evidence chapter, attributed to Canada
No control, no owner, no frequency
No metric in the barometer or control tower
No criterion in the quality gate

body.v: Six moves, and the last is the operable one. The instrument is the Guide on the Use of Agentic Artificial Intelligence, published by the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat on 22 May 2026, sitting on top of a directive that already made assessment mandatory.

kids.v: Named the risk inside an instrument

Continued offloading of decisions to AI agents can lead to knowledge and skill atrophy and weakened human judgment. Employees become less practiced at core tasks and slower to notice when something is wrong.
Guide on the Use of Agentic AI, TBS, 22 May 2026
Tied it to the validity of oversight

Maintenance of relevant skill sets among agentic AI users and deployers is treated as a prerequisite for meaningful human oversight. Not a wellbeing concern — a validity condition on the control itself.
Bounded autonomy and recoverability, introduced alongside the existing generative-AI principles rather than replacing them.
Service quality, privacy and security, legal defensibility and public trust. The risk is framed as legal and operational exposure, not a training preference.
Algorithmic Impact Assessment before deployment, four impact levels, external peer review at levels III and IV, questionnaire published openly including on GitHub.
Periodic human-only execution of agent-handled tasks for comparison; staff trained to interrogate agent outputs rather than accept them.

Canada names skill maintenance as a prerequisite for meaningful human oversight. A prerequisite that nobody measures is a sentiment. Aviation, nuclear operations and clinical practice all solved this the same way: recency requirements, evidenced, with authority attached. If you supervise the work, you stay current in the work. Six components, all of them auditable.

items.v: A reviewer executes an agent-handled task unaided, then compares. Tier 1 monthly, tier 2 quarterly, tier 3 twice yearly.
A reviewer whose last unaided execution predates the tier window loses approval authority on that queue until re-current. Enforced, not advised.
Every drill records agreement or disagreement and why. Sustained perfect agreement is itself a signal — it is what rubber-stamping looks like from outside.
Proportion of agent outputs materially amended before acceptance. A falling challenge rate against a flat error rate is drift, not improvement.
No reviewer supervises the same agent-handled queue continuously. Rotation preserves unaided practice somewhere in the role.
The register records which skills the agent displaces, who must retain them and to what standard. If nobody is named, the deployment is not approvable.
Register field, tested at each gate

kids.v: The uncomfortable component is the divergence log. A reviewer who agrees with the agent every time is either supervising a perfect agent or not supervising at all, and the record cannot tell the difference. Convergence has to be read as a warning rather than a result.

body.v: Eight instruments elsewhere, measured against ours
Three are outright gaps: something binding or published elsewhere with no UK counterpart. Four are partial. One is context we should track rather than copy.

items.v: AI Act Article 4 — the AI literacy duty

Binding since 2 February 2025 and unaffected by the proposed high-risk delay. Applies to deployers of every AI system, not only high-risk ones, and covers staff and contractors regardless of seniority. The compliance test is a dated, role-mapped programme that plausibly matches actual use.

kids.v: Training is encouraged throughout UK guidance but is nowhere a duty, and course completion is not evidence of competence.

items.v: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI

World-first agentic framework, Davos 22 January 2026; version 1.5 on 20 May 2026 after feedback from over sixty organisations, with more than ten deployment case studies. Four pillars, unique agent identities tied to a supervising agent or user, threat modelling for memory poisoning, tool misuse and privilege compromise.

kids.v: We hold secure-AI guidance and our own patterns, but no single agentic instrument and no agent identity requirement.

items.v: Directive on Automated Decision-Making, plus the agentic guide

Assessment is mandatory before deployment, scored across four impact levels, with external peer review at the top two. The questionnaire is published openly, including on GitHub, and has become the instrument others copy.

kids.v: ATRS is transparency after the fact, not assessment before it, and it is not a gate.

items.v: AI Safety Institute inaugural report, 9 August 2026

Found that NIST's risk framework, OWASP's Agentic Top 10, Singapore's agentic framework and ASD's agentic guidance all rest on the same hidden assumption: that one organisation owns every agent in a system. Cross-organisational agent risk is a structural gap none of them covers.

kids.v: Our register assumes single-owner agents too. The gap is identified and unimplemented everywhere, including here — which makes it available.

items.v: Singapore Consensus companion report on agentic risk

Ten foundational principles for managing agentic risk: least privilege, traceable identity, auditability, validated deployment, adversarial resilience, multi-agent stability, runtime assurance, interruptibility, legibility and human oversight.

kids.v: We hold most of these as scattered controls. None is consolidated into a named principle set an approver can test a deployment against.

items.v: Thirty-two of thirty-six countries run AI training programmes; only thirteen of thirty-six train on using AI in public services or in policymaking. Broad capability is improving faster than role-specific readiness. Thirty of thirty-six have an institution governing public-sector AI; twenty-one of thirty-six offer central procurement support.

kids.v: Our academy is role-based on paper. Depth of oversight-specific training has never been tested against this benchmark.

items.v: GAIN network and the GovAI Grand Challenge
A G7 AI network convened and chaired by Canada, tasked with a roadmap to scale successful public-sector AI projects and a catalogue of open-source, shareable AI solutions for members.

kids.v: We participate. We have contributed no reusable instrument to the catalogue.

items.v: Korea AI Basic Act (2026), Taiwan AI Basic Act (2025)
Regional convergence on human oversight, data safeguards and prohibitions on harmful or deceptive use, arriving through basic law rather than sectoral guidance.

kids.v: Context rather than gap: the UK route is guidance-led by choice. Worth tracking for interoperability, not imitation.

body.v: Thirteen items and three deliberate refusals. Every item has an owner and a first deliverable, because an unowned backlog item is a wish.

items.v: This quarter. Each one closes a gap that leaves an existing control unsound.

kids.v: Manual-mode drills, currency windows, divergence log, rotation and the displaced-skill register field. Turns the Canada finding into something an auditor can test.

First: Control spec and tier windows

kids.v: A dated, role-mapped competence requirement for anyone who operates or approves an agent, contractors in scope. The Article 4 test, applied voluntarily and ahead of any obligation.
Every agent carries a unique identity bound to a named human owner and, where orchestrated, to a supervising agent. Prerequisite for audit, for handover and for retirement.

items.v: First: Identity schema in the register

kids.v: Adopt both as named approval principles. Every agent has a tested interrupt and a tested rollback before it goes live, with the test evidenced.

items.v: First: Two gate criteria and a test script

kids.v: Challenge rate and divergence surfaced in the control tower beside assurance status, per queue, monthly.

items.v: Next two quarters. These extend reach rather than repair a fault.

kids.v: Register fields for agents we interact with but do not own: supplier, other department, arm's-length body. The first implementation of the gap Australia named.

items.v: First: Field set and one worked case

Not general AI awareness. Training in interrogating outputs, recognising plausible-but-wrong, and running a manual-mode drill.
A scored pre-deployment assessment distinct from the transparency record, with independent peer review at the top tiers.
Memory poisoning, tool misuse and privilege compromise added to the agent threat model and to the security review.

items.v: Worth doing, sequenced behind the above. This is where the leadership case is actually made.

kids.v: Register schema, gate criteria and the currency control released openly under the Open Government Licence, versioned, as Canada did with its assessment.
One partner nation, one deployment class, mutual recognition of assurance evidence. Tests whether our evidence travels before we offer it widely.

kids.v: Longitudinal measurement of unaided performance in agent-supported roles, with an academic partner. Nobody holds this data, which is why everyone is asserting rather than measuring.

items.v: Named, so the omission reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

kids.v: Not ours to set. We build the evidence base a policy decision would need.
The guidance route moves faster, and we do not yet hold the evidence to legislate well.
Capacity we do not have. Contract terms and evidence requirements instead.

body.v: Four things nobody has published yet

Parity is a floor, and reaching it puts us level with instruments already a year old. Each of these is a control we could be first to publish, and three of the four came out of our own case work rather than the international scan.

kids.v: Oversight currency as a revocable authority

Canada names skill maintenance as a prerequisite for oversight. Nobody has made it measurable and revocable — an approval right you can lose by going stale. Publishing the control with tier windows and drill records would be first.

Machinery-of-government change moves an owner; active agent work continues unattended and is later inherited by a team that never approved it. No framework surveyed handles ownership transfer on reorganisation.
Approval capacity treated as a finite, costed resource and rationed by risk tier, so review is real where it matters instead of uniform and hollow everywhere.

Australia's institute named cross-organisational agent risk as a gap no framework covers. A register field plus a handshake at departmental and supplier boundaries would be the first implementation of it.
Keeping pace is a rhythm, not a document
Four of the eight instruments above were published or revised in the last eight months. A guide refreshed annually is a guide that is wrong for eleven of them.
Horizon scan into the guidance ticker: new instrument, new version, new enforcement action.
Instrument diff across the eight tracked jurisdictions. What changed, what it obliges, whether it touches a control we hold.
Re-MoSCoW the backlog. Anything sitting in Should for two cycles is promoted or killed, never carried.
Publish the delta pack and contribute one reusable instrument to a shared catalogue.
Reciprocal review with a partner nation: they read our instruments, we read theirs, both publish the findings.
Where the work goes once it exists
Five routes already open to us. None of them takes a position paper; all of them take a working instrument.
The network's remit includes a catalogue of open-source, shareable AI solutions for members. A register schema and a currency control are exactly that shape.
OECD.AI and the Digital Government Outlook
The comparative baseline every country is measured against. Contributing method, rather than only returning survey answers, changes what the baseline measures.
The first binding international AI treaty, on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. The UK is a signatory, and the validity of human oversight sits squarely inside its scope.
The UK allocated roughly A$460m at the 2025 spending review, against about A$50m over five years in Canada and about A$11m a year in Singapore. Capacity to convene is not the constraint.
Open Government Licence v3.0, public repository, versioned. Canada published its assessment questionnaire openly and it became the reference others adopted.

chapters.title: Obligations register
chapters.heading: 164 obligations that bind AI use in UK public bodies
chapters.lede: Law, policy and guidance that apply when public servants use AI, across the four nations: data protection and transfers, records and FOI, security, equality, transparency, procurement, financial control, sustainability and more. Researched from primary sources in October 2026 and link-checked on 22 November 2026; check the source before you rely on any entry, because guidance changes. Not legal advice.

rows.v: What it means for AI use

Central government must default to public cloud (mandatory); it is strongly recommended for the wider public sector. The policy does not require UK data location: it allows services provided overseas or globally, subject to due diligence using ICO and NCSC guidance. SECRET and above is unlikely to suit public cloud. **Caveat:** Last updated 19 June 2023 on page history. 'UK-wide' here means UK central government; devolved administrations set their own policies.
GDS (DCMS) and Central Digital and Data Office
Scottish public sector cloud computing guidance (Scotland's Digital Future)

Positions cloud as a priority option and the intended dominant model for Scottish digital public services, covering central government, police and fire, local authorities, health and further/higher education. Scottish bodies choosing an AI service should check this alongside current Scottish Government digital guidance. **Caveat:** Dated 2015; whether it remains current Scottish Government policy is unconfirmed. Its data location content was not read. A gov.scot 'Cloud first' collection exists but returned no content.
[[https://www.gov.scot/publications/scotlands-digital-future-scottish-public-sector-cloud-computing-guidance/|Scotland's Digital Future: Scottish public sector cloud computing guidance]]

The main route for buying cloud and SaaS (including AI services) in the public sector. G-Cloud 15 adds Cyber Essentials (Plus for IaaS/PaaS lots), a lot for IaaS/PaaS above OFFICIAL, and terms closer to the Public Sector Contract. Buyers must still check data location and sub-processors in each service description and contract. **Caveat:** Anticipated award date was 17 Sep 2026; whether G15 is live and its data location clauses are unconfirmed. CCS primary documents not read.

[[https://www.burges-salmon.com/articles/102lzf5/g-cloud-15-g15-framework-key-changes-for-uk-public-sector-cloud-suppliers/|G-Cloud 15 (G15) framework: key changes for UK public sector cloud suppliers (Burges Salmon)]]
What it means for AI use

The four values (integrity, honesty, objectivity, impartiality) apply to everything you produce with AI help. You must set out facts truthfully, correct errors promptly, keep accurate official records and not disclose official information without authority, so AI output must be checked before it informs advice, and official information must not be put into tools not authorised to hold it. Special advisers are covered except for objectivity and impartiality. **Caveat:** The code does not mention AI; applying it to AI use is an interpretation. Scottish and Welsh Government have their own versions (see separate items).
Cabinet Office (Civil Service Commission hears complaints)

Welsh Government civil servants are part of the Home Civil Service and follow a Welsh Government version of the Code with the same four values. The same duties on truthful advice, accurate records and protecting official information govern AI-assisted work. **Caveat:** Page dated 2017 (document labelled January 2017); no AI-specific content.

Scottish Government civil servants are part of the Home Civil Service; the GB Code states the Scottish Government and its agencies have their own version of the Code with the same core values. Treat AI-assisted work as subject to the same duties of honesty, objectivity and confidentiality. **Caveat:** Current gov.scot URL for the Scottish version was not retrieved; only an archived copy surfaced. Existence confirmed via the GB Code's own text; current text unverified.
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/civil-service-code/the-civil-service-code|The Civil Service Code (gov.uk) - note on Scottish and Welsh versions]]

Northern Ireland civil servants follow the NICS Code of Ethics: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. It requires accurate official records, prompt correction of factual errors, openness within the law and no unauthorised disclosure, so AI outputs must be verified and official information kept out of unapproved tools. **Caveat:** First published February 2022, revised May 2024, reviewed annually each February; a later revision may exist. No AI-specific text.
Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government

The main cross-government guidance for civil servants using or building AI, built on 10 principles: know what AI is and its limits; use it lawfully, ethically and responsibly; use it securely; keep meaningful human control; manage the full lifecycle; use the right tool; be open and collaborative; involve commercial colleagues early; have the right skills; and use the principles alongside your organisation's policies and assurance. End users are responsible for checking outputs for accuracy, fairness and legal compliance, and accountability rests with the organisation. **Caveat:** No visible 2026 revision or successor found as of 19 Oct 2026, despite the July 2026 machinery change. Written for central government but offered to the wider public sector; devolved governments use it alongside their own guidance.
Published by Government Digital Service; AI adoption policy now led by Cabinet Office (from 21 July 2026); GDS now in DCMS
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government|Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government]]
Withdrawn on 10 February 2025 and replaced by the AI Playbook. Do not cite it as current guidance; update local policies that still refer to it.
Guidance to civil servants on use of generative AI (2023, superseded)

The 2023 guidance told staff never to put classified, sensitive or policy-revealing information or personal data into public generative AI tools, and to cite AI output. It has been superseded (first by the Generative AI Framework, now by the AI Playbook), but its basic rule still reflects current practice in departmental policies. **Caveat:** The page is marked superseded rather than formally withdrawn; 'Withdrawn' status here means 'no longer current'.
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidance-to-civil-servants-on-use-of-generative-ai/guidance-to-civil-servants-on-use-of-generative-ai|Guidance to civil servants on use of generative AI]]

A series of short technical explainers that sit alongside the AI Playbook, covering LLM bias, prompt engineering and prompt risks, agentic AI, RAG, AI coding assistants, synthetic data and model distillation. Use them for practical, topic-specific guidance; they do not replace departmental policy. **Caveat:** Last updated 3 August 2026 (15 titles at that date). Publisher listed as DCMS and GDS after the July 2026 machinery change.
Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and Government Digital Service
The People Factor and the Mitigating Hidden AI Risks Toolkit

Cabinet Office guidance drawn from scaling the in-house Assist tool. It sets out six 'hidden' risk areas: quality assurance, task-tool mismatch, perceptions and signalling, workflow challenges, ethics, and over-reliance. It recommends giving teams secure access to approved tools and knowing how general tools are being used, which is the closest central guidance to managing unsanctioned ('shadow') AI. **Caveat:** Does not address personal or consumer AI accounts as a distinct issue.
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/a-human-centred-approach-to-scaling-and-de-risking-ai-tools|A human-centred approach to scaling and de-risking AI tools]]
Staff use of personal or consumer AI tools ('shadow AI') - central position

No current, published cross-government rule specifically on staff using personal or consumer AI accounts for work was found. In practice the position comes from departmental security and acceptable-use policies, the Civil Service Code and data protection law: do not enter official, sensitive or personal information into tools your organisation has not approved, and follow your organisation's policies (AI Playbook principle 10). **Caveat:** This item records a gap, not a published instrument. Devolved administrations have their own internal rules (see the Welsh Government SIRO notice, Scottish Government and NICS items).
Cabinet Office (AI adoption) with departmental SIROs

[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html|AI Playbook principle 10; Guidance to civil servants on use of generative AI (2023)]]
Scottish Government generative AI guidance for staff

Scottish Government staff guidance (made public through FOI) tells officials not to put sensitive material into AI tools, including unreleased announcements, and to apply the test 'do not share anything you would not be happy to share with a member of the public'. Staff must fact-check outputs, avoid prompts that hint at future policy, and assess whether a paid tool protects submitted information. **Caveat:** Secondary source reporting an FOI release; the guidance itself is internal and its date and title are not published. A Scottish Government FOI response (April 2025) confirms general generative AI guidance is 'available to all staff'.

[[https://www.publictechnology.net/2025/05/15/science-technology-and-research/gen-ai-guidance-tells-scottish-officials-do-not-share-anything-you-would-not-share-with-a-member-of-the-public/|Gen AI guidance tells Scottish officials do not share anything you would not share with a member of the public (PublicTechnology, reporting FOI release)]]
Welsh Government SIRO Notice 2024/002: ChatGPT and generative AI tools

Welsh Government staff may use only Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot for Bing with OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE information. They must not enter OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or personal information into other tools such as ChatGPT, must take care discussing Welsh Government business in any AI tool (including on personal accounts), and must check all output. Buying AI licences or adding AI features needs Solution Design Authority approval. **Caveat:** Internal notice released through FOI in November 2025; it may since have been updated.
NICS Policy on the Use of (Generative) AI

The Northern Ireland Civil Service has a policy on the use of generative AI, adopted in June 2024, that governs responsible and ethical AI use across departments. Microsoft Copilot was rolled out to staff in at least one department (Infrastructure) in December 2025. Departmental SIROs approve AI use (for example in The Executive Office). **Caveat:** Policy text not publicly retrieved; existence and date come from Assembly written answers (June 2026), reproduced on an MLA's website. An earlier NICS generative AI guidance dates from mid-2023.
What it means for AI use
Generative AI and Crown copyright: a brief guide for government departments

Work that civil servants create with generative AI in the course of their duties, and then review, modify and assure, may be Crown copyright. Where a provider's terms give the user ownership of outputs, those outputs belong to the Crown. If the terms assign outputs to the provider, seek legal advice. Departments must still publish attribution and licensing statements and attribute third-party material. **Caveat:** No exact publication date; the copyright notice is 2025.
[[https://cdn.nationalarchives.gov.uk/documents/ai-crown-copyright.pdf|Generative AI and Crown copyright: A brief guide for government departments]]
Open Government Licence and AI training on government content

Most Crown copyright material is published under the OGL, which allows it to be used to train AI models provided the licence terms, including attribution, are followed. Departments holding a delegation of authority to license on other terms must check whether AI providers' terms affect that licensing. **Caveat:** The OGL itself predates generative AI. TNA's view on training is guidance, not a court ruling.
[[https://cdn.nationalarchives.gov.uk/documents/ai-crown-copyright.pdf|Generative AI and Crown copyright: A brief guide for government departments]]
Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (DUAA ss.135-136)

The government no longer prefers a broad text and data mining exception with a rightsholder opt-out, and has not chosen an alternative. It will gather more evidence, explore output labelling and digital replica rights, and keep protection for computer-generated works under review. There is no change to copyright law yet, so public bodies using AI must respect third-party copyright under existing law. **Caveat:** No legislative timetable. A digital replicas consultation was expected in summer 2026 and its publication is unconfirmed. The post-July 2026 owner department for copyright policy is unconfirmed.
Published by DSIT, DCMS and the Intellectual Property Office; IP policy now with BIST/IPO (post-July 2026, unconfirmed) (DSIT, abolished 21 July 2026; check the successor owner)
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/report-and-impact-assessment-on-copyright-and-artificial-intelligence|Report and impact assessment on copyright and artificial intelligence]]
What it means for AI use
UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018

Any AI tool that processes personal data (in prompts, uploaded files, grounding data or outputs) is subject to UK GDPR and the DPA 2018. Data protection is reserved in Scotland and Northern Ireland and is a specific reservation for Wales, so the same law applies across the UK; devolved bodies follow it but have their own records and FOI regimes. **Caveat:** Explanatory notes say Scotland Act Sch 5 Pt II B2 and NI Act Sch 3 para 40 make it reserved; Wales Act 2017 adds a specific reservation (para 170). Amended by DUAA 2025 from 2025-2026.
Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)
Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 — commencement status

Most data protection reforms commenced on 5 February 2026 (Commencement No. 6, SI 2026/82), including the new transfer regime, recognised legitimate interests and the new automated decision-making Articles 22A-D. The complaints duty started on 19 June 2026 and the Information Commission replaced the ICO on 30 September 2026. Check commencement before relying on any individual provision. **Caveat:** Earlier commencement orders: No.1 20 Aug 2025, No.3 5 Sep/17 Nov 2025, No.4 1 Dec 2025 (per Kennedys, grade B). Whether every remaining section has now commenced is unconfirmed; the departmental owner of data protection policy after July 2026 is inferred from the DCMS-published Information Commission release.
DCMS (UK data policy since the July 2026 machinery of government change); regulator: Information Commission
