Chatbots and voice systems must give an equivalent Welsh service, and AI-delivered training, recruitment and performance tools must not disadvantage Welsh speakers. The Commissioner will run periodic audits. **Caveat:** Publication date inferred from the PDF filename (20250722); the page shows no date.

[[https://www.welshlanguagecommissioner.wales/regulation/promoting-compliance/artificial-intelligence-and-the-welsh-language-the-welsh-language-commissioners-regulatory-policy-statement|Artificial Intelligence and the Welsh language: the Welsh Language Commissioner's Regulatory Policy Statement]]
Gaelic Language (Scotland) Act 2005 as amended by the Scottish Languages Act 2025

Scottish public authorities with Gaelic language plans must deliver the measures in their plans, which can include digital and automated services. The 2025 Act lets Ministers set Gaelic standards by regulation, adds areas of linguistic significance and requires annual reporting. Bodies with plans should consider Gaelic provision when introducing AI-delivered services such as chatbots and translation. **Caveat:** The Act is being commenced in stages: areas of linguistic significance from 21 March 2026 (Eilean Siar), 1 September 2026 (Highland, Argyll and Bute) and 1 January 2027 (all other areas). Gaelic standards regulations had not been confirmed as made by 19 Oct 2026. No Bòrd guidance specific to AI was found.
[[https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2025/10/part/1/enacted|Scottish Languages Act 2025, Part 1; Commencement No. 2 Regulations 2026 (SSI 2026/128)]]
Identity and Language (Northern Ireland) Act 2022 - Irish language and Ulster Scots commissioners

The Act created an Irish Language Commissioner, who can set best-practice standards for public authorities and investigate complaints, and a Commissioner for Ulster Scots and the Ulster British tradition. The first commissioners took up post on 13 November 2025. NI public authorities should expect standards that may cover digital and AI-delivered services, but none were confirmed as of October 2026. **Caveat:** No standards or AI-specific guidance from either commissioner found as of 19 Oct 2026. TEO page last updated 19 August 2026.
The Executive Office (NI); Office of Identity and Cultural Expression
Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018 - WCAG 2.2 AA

Public sector websites and apps, including AI chatbots and AI-generated content published on them, must meet WCAG 2.2 level AA and publish an accessibility statement. GDS monitors compliance. Enforcement is by the EHRC in Great Britain and the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland. **Caveat:** The Regulations are a UK SI; the monitoring page names enforcers for all four nations but does not state the extent explicitly. Applying them to AI chatbots is inferred from the scope of websites and apps.
Government Digital Service (monitoring, now in DCMS); EHRC and ECNI (enforcement)
[[https://www.gov.uk/guidance/public-sector-website-and-mobile-application-accessibility-monitoring|Public sector website and mobile application accessibility monitoring]]

body.v: Local government and wider public sector (8)

rows.v: What it means for AI use

Resources for English councils: a playbook for agentic AI in local government (October 2026), 'AI in Local Government: What Councillors Need to Know' (September 2026), a Responsibly buying AI procurement guide, a case study bank and a 1,000+ member AI Community of Practice. A Local Government AI Playbook and AI governance templates are planned for 2026/27. **Caveat:** Hub page; individual resource dates as listed on it.
MHCLG Local AI team and responsible AI adoption programme for councils

MHCLG's Local AI team builds reusable AI tools for councils, such as a transcription tool based on i.AI's Minute. It funds the LGA to co-deliver an AI maturity playbook, standard assessment templates that combine data protection and equality checks, a minimum standard for responsible AI and an AI policy template. **Caveat:** Products (playbook, templates, minimum standard) were in development at July 2026. Scope is English councils (MHCLG remit) but not stated explicitly.
Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government
[[https://mhclgdigital.blog.gov.uk/2026/07/13/from-engagement-to-delivery-supporting-responsible-ai-adoption-in-councils/|From engagement to delivery: supporting responsible AI adoption in councils]]
Interim Guidance on the use of AI in Health and Social Care (Scotland) - with COSLA and Digital Office

Joint Scottish Government, COSLA and Digital Office guidance to NHS boards, councils and Health and Social Care Partnerships. It asks for an AI oversight group, Data Ethics Boards in local authorities, early trade union engagement, human oversight of decisions affecting people, and lifecycle risk management. Staff remain accountable for AI-assisted work, and organisations remain accountable for AI scribes. **Caveat:** Interim, ahead of a full AI Policy Framework. Copy retrieved from an NHS Highland-hosted site, not gov.scot. No standalone COSLA AI guidance for all council services was found.
Scottish Government (DG Health and Social Care), COSLA, Digital Office for Scottish Local Government

[[https://www.communitypharmacy.scot.nhs.uk/nhs-highland/wp-content/uploads/sites/12/Scot-Gov-AI-Interim-Guidance-on-the-use-of-AI-in-health-and-social-care-August-2026-Signed-Final.pdf|Interim Guidance on the use of AI in Health and Social Care (letter, 17 Aug 2026)]]
WLGA and Welsh local government AI

WLGA sits on the Welsh Government's Strategic AI Advisory Group, and the Welsh Government has funded guidance for local authorities on deploying AI. Welsh councils also follow the Workforce Partnership Council AI guidance, Welsh Language Standards and the Socio-economic Duty when adopting AI. **Caveat:** No WLGA-published AI guidance was found. Publication of the funded local authority guidance is unconfirmed.
Welsh Local Government Association; Welsh Government
NILGA AI resources for councillors (Northern Ireland)

NILGA provides Copilot for Councillors training (briefing and webinar) on responsible use of Microsoft Copilot and points councillors to the LGA AI Unpacked videos. No NI-wide AI policy framework for councils was found. **Caveat:** Date inferred from file names (late January 2026), not stated on the page.
NHS England guidance on AI-enabled ambient scribing products

NHS organisations in England adopting AI scribes should follow this guidance, which has separate summaries for boards, CIOs and CCIOs and technical teams, and the companion information governance guidance (March 2026). It covers medical device status, clinical safety and data protection. **Caveat:** Latest component (CIO/CCIO summary v3) dated 29 July 2026. NHS England is being merged into DHSC; ownership may change.
[[https://www.england.nhs.uk/publication/guidance-on-the-use-of-ai-enabled-ambient-scribing-products/|Guidance on the use of AI-enabled ambient scribing products in health and care settings]]
NHS Wales: safe and responsible adoption of ambient voice technologies (WHC/2025/026)

A Welsh Health Circular telling NHS Wales bodies how to adopt AI scribes safely and responsibly in clinical settings. NHS Wales staff and digital teams should follow it before piloting or buying ambient voice tools. **Caveat:** Detailed requirements were not read in this check.
[[https://www.gov.wales/node/70116|The safe and responsible adoption of ambient voice technologies (AI scribes) in clinical settings (WHC/2025/026)]]

A shared, practical starting point for HSC organisations in Northern Ireland to use AI safely, ethically and responsibly. It promotes safety, transparency, fairness and human oversight. It is described as a living document, not a policy or strategy. **Caveat:** Issue date taken from the PDF filename (FINAL 280126); page last updated 2 April 2026.
Digital Health and Care Northern Ireland (DHCNI)
What it means for AI use
Machinery of government change: DSIT abolished, AI policy moved to Cabinet Office

From 21 July 2026, AI strategy, public sector AI adoption and the AI Security Institute moved to the Cabinet Office. A new AI Taskforce sits in the Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet. GDS moved to an expanded DCMS, and science and innovation went to the renamed Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST). Check that documents citing DSIT ownership still have a current owner. **Caveat:** The fact sheet does not say where i.AI, data policy, ATRS or the Responsible Technology Adoption Unit now sit. The acronym was changed from DBIST to BIST on 27 July 2026.
Cabinet Office / Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet
AI Opportunities Action Plan (and One Year On report)

The UK's 50-recommendation plan (January 2025) to grow AI capability and drive adoption, including across the public sector. The January 2026 progress report says 38 of the 50 commitments have been met. Public sector AI adoption under the plan is now led by the Cabinet Office. **Caveat:** Original plan published 13 Jan 2025; the One Year On report 29 Jan 2026. Public-sector-specific recommendations were not re-read in this check.
Published by DSIT (abolished); now Cabinet Office for AI strategy
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-opportunities-action-plan-one-year-on|AI Opportunities Action Plan: One Year On]]

The government body that researches the risks of advanced AI and develops and tests mitigations. Since 21 July 2026 it sits with the Cabinet Office. Its work informs security expectations for frontier models that departments may use; it does not regulate departmental AI use. **Caveat:** The gov.uk organisation page did not yet name a parent department when checked. The 2025 rename date (from AI Safety Institute) was not re-verified.
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/ai-security-institute/about|AI Security Institute - About (gov.uk); Machinery of government changes: fact sheet]]
Incubator for Artificial Intelligence (i.AI) - part of GDS

i.AI builds shared AI tools for government, such as the Humphrey suite and Minute, which MHCLG is adapting for councils. It became part of GDS in January 2025. Use i.AI tools through your organisation's approved routes. **Caveat:** Whether i.AI stayed with GDS in DCMS or moved to the Cabinet Office AI function after July 2026 is not confirmed by any source found.
Government Digital Service (now in DCMS) - post-July 2026 home unconfirmed

Scotland's five-year AI strategy is principles-based, follows the OECD AI Principles and rests on Fair Work. It is delivered through the AI Scotland programme, with ten actions due by March 2027, including embedding ethical AI frameworks in health and social care. It replaces the 2021 strategy delivered through the Scottish AI Alliance. **Caveat:** Published before the May 2026 Scottish Parliament election; how the new government is delivering it after the election has not been confirmed.
Scotland Digital Strategy delivery plan 2025-2028: ethical AI framework and public sector AI actions

Commits the Scottish Government to an ethical AI framework in 2026, offering a library of approved frameworks plus a policy statement on ethical public sector AI use. It also commits to AI pilots in operations, a public sector working group on AI adoption and ethics, and, for local government, a national AI governance framework, Technical Assurance Group and national AI registry by 2028. **Caveat:** Publication of the ethical AI framework (due 2026) not confirmed by 19 Oct 2026.
Scottish Government and Digital Office for Scottish Local Government

[[https://www.gov.scot/publications/digital-strategy-scotland-sustainable-digital-public-services-delivery-plan-2025-2028/pages/6/|Digital strategy for Scotland: sustainable digital public services - delivery plan 2025-2028]]

An open, plain-language guide from the Scottish AI Alliance for organisations starting with AI. It covers strategy, procurement and governance, and is supported by a practitioner community, workshops and case studies. Use it alongside Scottish Government and UK guidance. **Caveat:** Described via a Data Lab case study; the playbook site was not fetched. Its upkeep after the 2021 strategy ended in 2026 is unconfirmed.
Scottish AI Alliance / The Data Lab
[[https://thedatalab.com/case-studies/scottish-ai-alliance-leading-scotlands-ai-strategy/|Scottish AI Alliance: leading Scotland's AI strategy (case study)]]
AI Cymru: AI Plan for Wales

The Welsh Government's AI plan includes quick wins to roll out AI training across the Welsh public sector, improve Welsh-language speech and language technology, and deliver services in English and Welsh. It is supported by a new Office for AI and a Strategic AI Advisory Group whose members include WLGA and Wales TUC. **Caveat:** Detailed commitments are taken from UKAuthority's report (20 Nov 2025), as the gov.wales landing page does not list them.
Written Statement: AI and digital transformation in Welsh public services

The Welsh Government set up an Office for AI and a Strategic AI Advisory Group, funded guidance for local authorities and others on deploying AI, funded AI training for public sector workers and an evaluation of AI scribes, and is building a platform for testing AI tools. It also confirmed that CDPS functions are being brought into the Welsh Government. **Caveat:** Whether the CDPS integration was completed by April 2026 is unconfirmed.

[[https://www.gov.wales/written-statement-artificial-intelligence-and-digital-transformation-welsh-public-services|Written Statement: Artificial Intelligence and digital transformation in Welsh public services]]
Northern Ireland draft Artificial Intelligence Strategy

The Executive Office's draft strategy for responsible AI adoption across the NI public sector proposes eight principles: human oversight, accountability and redress, data governance, technical safety and security, fairness and transparency, sustainability, societal benefit, and training and literacy. Consultation runs from 12 August to 4 November 2026. **Caveat:** Draft only; the final strategy may change.
The Executive Office (NI) - Office of AI & Digital
[[https://www.executiveoffice-ni.gov.uk/consultations/northern-irelands-draft-artificial-intelligence-strategy|Northern Ireland's Draft Artificial Intelligence Strategy - consultation]]
What it means for AI use
**England, Wales, Northern Ireland**. Law, In force

The public procurement regime for procurements started on or after 24 February 2025 by contracting authorities in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, with the Procurement Regulations 2024. It changes notices, transparency, exclusions and contract management for every AI purchase above threshold. It applies to devolved Welsh and transferred NI authorities with some differences, but generally not to devolved Scottish authorities, which stay under Scottish law. **Caveat:** Procurement is devolved; this UK Act applies to reserved, Welsh and NI authorities by agreement, so reserved_or_devolved is n/a. Royal Assent date from general knowledge, not re-checked today. The NI Department of Finance PPN page lists no Act-specific PPNs (checked 19 Oct 2026).
Procurement Act guidance: devolved contracting authorities

Explains which parts of the Procurement Act apply in each nation. Devolved Welsh authorities follow the Wales Procurement Policy Statement instead of the National Procurement Policy Statement (in force 24 February 2025, which other covered authorities must 'have regard to'). Transferred NI authorities are exempt from the NPPS except under reserved arrangements. Devolved Scottish authorities generally follow Scottish law unless buying jointly with, or through a framework of, a UK, Welsh or NI authority. **Caveat:** Last updated 15 April 2026.
Procurement Reform (Scotland) Act 2014 and cross-border regulations

Devolved Scottish authorities buy AI under the Procurement Reform (Scotland) Act 2014 and Scottish procurement regulations, not the Procurement Act 2023. From 20 December 2025 the Cross-Border Public Procurement (Miscellaneous Amendment) (Scotland) Regulations 2025 largely disapply Scottish rules when a Scottish authority buys through a UK framework (for example a Government Commercial Agency agreement), so most of the Procurement Act's relevant provisions apply instead. **Caveat:** Commencement date and regulation title come from a law-firm summary (DWF, January 2026); the SPPN 5/2026 page text could not be read. SSI number not confirmed.

[[https://www.gov.scot/publications/public-procurement-cross-border-co-operation-within-the-uk-sppn-5-2026/|Guidance: Devolved Contracting Authorities; Public procurement – cross-border co-operation within the UK: SPPN 5/2026]]
Wales: Procurement (Wales) Regulations 2024 and Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023

Welsh contracting authorities use the Procurement Act 2023 with the Procurement (Wales) Regulations 2024 (e.g. contract details notices above £30,000 including VAT) and must have regard to the Wales Procurement Policy Statement. Socially responsible procurement duties under the Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023 commenced in stages, including provisions from 21 March 2025. When Welsh bodies call off UK frameworks (e.g. Government Commercial Agency), UK rules apply to that call-off. **Caveat:** There is no 'Procurement (Wales) Act 2024'. The 2024 Welsh Act is the Health Service Procurement (Wales) Act 2024, which lets Welsh Ministers disapply the Procurement Act for NHS Wales health services.
[[https://www.gov.wales/node/79239|WPPN 018: Publication of contract details notices for call-offs under legacy arrangements]]
PPN 017: Improving transparency of AI use in procurement

For procurements started on or after 24 February 2025, central government departments, agencies and NDPBs should consider asking suppliers to disclose AI use in bids (non-scored questions), carry out proportionate due diligence on AI-written tenders, stop suppliers using confidential or non-public authority data to train AI, and plan for longer timelines. Where AI might be used to deliver a 'non-AI' service, consider requiring suppliers to declare it and set contract terms on use of data such as meeting transcripts. PPN 02/24 still applies to procurements started before that date. **Caveat:** Other public bodies 'may' apply it. Does not address devolved application. PPN 02/24 page (25 March 2024) has a 9 Sept 2026 metadata update with no visible change.

[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ppn-017-improving-transparency-of-ai-use-in-procurement/ppn-017-improving-transparency-of-ai-use-in-procurement-html|PPN 017: Improving transparency of AI use in procurement]]

From 1 October 2025, central government departments, agencies and NDPBs must give social value at least 10% of the total score in procurements under the Procurement Act (with listed exclusions). Outcomes are organised around government missions, including Outcome 4 'sustainable procurement' – a natural home for AI energy and carbon commitments in AI contracts. **Caveat:** Does not apply below threshold, to MOD defence and security contracts or to private utilities. Wales uses its own social value / community benefits notes (e.g. WPPN 003).

[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ppn-002-taking-account-of-social-value-in-the-award-of-contracts/ppn-002-taking-account-of-social-value-in-the-award-of-central-government-contracts-html|PPN 002: Taking account of social value in the award of central government contracts]]

G-Cloud 15 replaced G-Cloud 14 from 6 August 2026 and is an open framework under the Procurement Act 2023. Lots cover IaaS/PaaS (at and above OFFICIAL), infrastructure SaaS, other SaaS and cloud support – the main route for buying AI services sold as cloud software. Call-off contracts can run up to 60 months; new suppliers can join at reopening windows. **Caveat:** Agreement page lists end date 5 February 2028 but describes a 4-year term – inconsistent; confirm before relying. No AI-specific lot.
[[https://www.gca.gov.uk/agreements/RM1557.15|G-Cloud 15 agreement page; 'G-Cloud relaunches with biggest upgrade in its history']]

The Government Commercial Agency's dynamic purchasing system for AI services – discovery, consultancy, licensing, implementation, support and end-to-end partnerships, including medical AI for health bodies. It was extended in November 2025 to 23 February 2029 while a replacement is designed; contracts can last up to 4 years. **Caveat:** Extension notice published 21 November 2025 (Find a Tender 2025/S 000-076043). No successor agreement named.
Microsoft SPA24 memorandum of understanding (incl. Copilot)

A five-year MoU from 1 November 2024 replacing DTA21, giving eligible public sector bodies better pricing across Microsoft products, including Microsoft 365, Azure and Copilot. Crown Commercial Service became the Government Commercial Agency on 1 April 2026; existing agreements continue under gca.gov.uk. It is pricing, not a contract: you still need a compliant procurement route, and CCS/GCA recommends Technology Products & Associated Services 2 (RM6098, runs to 9 October 2027). **Caveat:** Discount levels and Copilot-specific terms are not public. Copilot inclusion confirmed by UKAuthority report (21 Oct 2024), not the GCA page.
[[https://www.gca.gov.uk/news/crown-commercial-service-signs-memorandum-understanding-microsoft-uk-spa24|Crown Commercial Service signs memorandum of understanding with Microsoft UK – SPA24]]

OGVA is a pan-public-sector discount MoU with Amazon Web Services; OGVA 1 (from October 2020) offered baseline discounts of up to 18%. OGVA 2.0 was renewed quietly in late 2023 as a three-year MoU, with departmental agreements starting 1 December 2023; its discounts were not published. Departments using it typically sign minimum-commit contracts, which create the same use-it-or-lose-it risk as prepaid AI capacity. **Caveat:** No primary government source found. Status after the three-year term (around late 2026) is unconfirmed; check with GCA.

[[https://computerweekly.com/news/366562418/UK-government-quietly-renews-public-sector-preferential-pricing-agreement-with-AWS|UK government quietly renews public sector preferential pricing agreement with AWS (Computer Weekly)]]
Google Cloud strategic partnership with UK government

Announced July 2025: Google Cloud support to modernise legacy public services and help departments exit 'ball and chain' contracts, training for up to 100,000 civil servants in tech and AI by 2030, and DeepMind collaboration. Commercial terms (discounts, duration, MoU status) were not published and the announcement says arrangements 'may be subject to future commercial agreements'. **Caveat:** Terms unconfirmed. No Oracle pan-government agreement status was verified in this research.
Cabinet Office (AI policy; announced by DSIT, now abolished)

[[https://www.gov.uk/government/news/new-google-partnership-will-help-rid-taxpayer-of-ball-and-chain-legacy-tech-and-aim-to-upskill-100000-civil-servants-in-tech-and-ai|New Google partnership will help rid taxpayer of 'ball and chain' legacy tech]]
Guidelines for AI procurement (Office for AI, 2020)

The original UK guidance on buying AI: start from the problem, run data assessments, plan for explainability, ethics and lifecycle governance, and avoid lock-in. It has not been withdrawn, but predates generative AI, the Procurement Act 2023 and PPN 017, so read it alongside the AI Playbook. **Caveat:** Content summary partly from general knowledge of the 2020 document; only status and dates were re-checked today.
Cabinet Office (AI policy; originally Office for AI, published by DSIT) (DSIT, abolished 21 July 2026; check the successor owner)
AI Playbook for the UK Government – commercial and cost principles

Principle 8 says to work with commercial colleagues from the start and hold suppliers to the same responsible-AI standards, using contract terms to require transparency. The buying section asks you to budget for hidden costs and plan strategies to avoid vendor lock-in; the cost section warns AI needs ongoing investment and can carry considerable compute costs. It also tells teams to understand and manage the environmental impact of AI and choose the most sustainable option that meets the need. **Caveat:** Its spend-control references (mandatory assurance above £100k public-facing) are out of date since 1 April 2026.
Government Digital Service (DCMS) / Cabinet Office AI policy
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html|Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government]]

Thirteen points for designing, building and buying technology, including be open and use open source (3), open standards (4), cloud first (5), share and reuse (8), define your purchasing strategy including contractual limitations (11) and make your technology sustainable across its lifecycle (12). Use it to test AI purchases for portability, reuse and exit. **Caveat:** Page still says TCoP is used for Cabinet Office spend control, which largely ended 1 April 2026; the Digital Assurance Playbook now cites it as guidance. The GOV.UK Service Standard has 14 points and none on sustainability.
Scottish Procurement Journey: Artificial Intelligence guidance

Scottish Government guidance for buyers and bidders on AI, published on the Procurement Journey and Supplier Journey sites. Responsible AI use is permitted in procurement for both, subject to each body's policies, with proportionate steps to manage risk. **Caveat:** Read via the Scottish Government blog announcement; the Procurement Journey pages themselves were not read.
Scottish Procurement Cloud and Hosting Services framework (SP-22-023)

National framework open to all Scottish public bodies (central government, health, councils, universities, colleges and eligible third sector) for cloud and hosting, by mini-competition or direct award, from 1 November 2023 to 31 October 2027. A Scotland-specific route for hosting AI workloads. **Caveat:** No AI-specific Scottish national framework was found.
[[https://www.gov.scot/publications/procurement-cloud-and-hosting-services-framework-sp-22-023/|Procurement – cloud and hosting services: framework SP-22-023]]
What it means for AI use
Freedom of Information Act 2000 — AI prompts and outputs are 'information'
**England, Wales, Northern Ireland**. Law, In force

FOIA covers 'information recorded in any form' held by a public authority, which includes AI prompts, outputs and chat histories held on work systems or in tools used for work. Treat AI interactions as potentially disclosable and searchable. Scottish public authorities are covered by FOISA instead; UK-wide bodies operating in Scotland remain under FOIA. **Caveat:** The reserved/devolved position for FOI in Wales and NI was not verified, so marked n/a. Related: ICO guidance on handling AI-generated FOI requests, 6 May 2026 (https://ico.org.uk/about-the-ico/media-centre/news-and-blogs/2026/05/new-guidance-to-support-public-authorities-dealing-with-ai-generated-foi-requests/).
Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)
ICO guidance: Freedom of information and artificial intelligence

If staff use AI for work, both the prompts and the AI-generated outputs are covered by FOIA when held. If a tool keeps conversation history, it must be searched when a request covers it. Move official information produced with AI into a corporate information management system with appropriate retention, and inaccurate AI content is not exempt just because it is wrong. **Caveat:** Publication date taken from page metadata. Addresses FOIA only, not EIR or private accounts specifically.
Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)
DSIT FOI responses on ministers' ChatGPT history (2025)

A precedent: in 2025 DSIT treated the Secretary of State's ChatGPT history used in an official capacity as information held under FOIA and released it (FOI2025-00120); a later request was refused under section 21 only because the material was already published. Assume official use of AI tools, including by ministers, can be requested. **Caveat:** This is a departmental FOI response, not a regulator decision notice. No ICO decision notice on AI chat logs was found. FOI2025-00120 itself not read.
DSIT (publisher at the time; department abolished 21 July 2026)
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/foi2025-00209-chatgpt-history-of-ministers-in-dsit/response-chatgpt-history-of-ministers-in-dsit|FOI2025-00209: ChatGPT history of ministers in DSIT]]
Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 and the Scottish Information Commissioner

Scottish public authorities answer to FOISA, which also defines information as 'recorded in any form', so AI prompts and outputs held for work are in scope. Appeals go to the Scottish Information Commissioner, who reported an 83% rise in appeals, many AI-generated, and issued requester guidance plus an appeal management policy; AI guidance for public bodies is forthcoming. **Caveat:** Commissioner's AI-related activity is from MFMac (10 Jul 2026, grade B); itspublicknowledge.info pages were not read. No SIC guidance confirming AI prompts are held information was found.
**England, Wales, Northern Ireland**. Regulation, In force

Environmental information (including policies, plans and analyses affecting the environment) recorded in any form is requestable under the EIR, not FOIA. AI-assisted analysis of environmental matters, and its prompts and outputs, may fall under the EIR. Scottish public authorities follow separate Scottish regulations. **Caveat:** Application to AI records is an inference from the definition; no ICO EIR-specific AI guidance was found. Scottish equivalent (EISR 2004) not read.
Information Commission (successor to the ICO from 30 Sept 2026)

Those responsible for public records must select records worth permanent preservation under the guidance of the Keeper (The National Archives) and transfer them, generally within 20 years. AI prompts and outputs that form part of the record of decisions should be captured in corporate systems so they can be appraised; transient AI drafts may not need keeping. **Caveat:** Geographic extent was not shown in the fetch; the Act covers UK government departments' records as well as English and Welsh public records. No TNA guidance specific to generative AI prompts was found.
Lord Chancellor's Code of Practice on the Management of Records (FOIA s.46)

Statutory code on keeping, managing and destroying records for public authorities in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Retention schedules and information asset registers should be updated to cover AI tool logs, prompts, outputs and embeddings. **Caveat:** The code predates generative AI; the AI-specific sentence is a recommended application.

[[https://gov.uk/government/publications/code-of-practice-on-the-management-of-records-issued-under-section-46-the-freedom-of-information-act-2000|Code of Practice on the management of records issued under section 46 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000]]
Public Records (Scotland) Act 2011 — records management plans

Named Scottish public authorities must prepare a records management plan, have it agreed by the Keeper of the Records of Scotland and manage records in line with it, covering responsibilities, security, retention, archiving and disposal. AI-generated records need to fit the agreed plan. **Caveat:** No National Records of Scotland guidance specific to AI found.
Keeper of the Records of Scotland (National Records of Scotland)
Public Records Act (Northern Ireland) 1923 and PRONI

Public records of NI courts, departments and authorities are governed by the 1923 Act and the Disposal of Documents Order 1925, which underpin disposal schedules and require a responsible records officer. PRONI receives and preserves records. AI records in NI bodies should be covered by disposal schedules. **Caveat:** No PRONI AI guidance found.
Public Record Office of Northern Ireland
[[https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/public-records-act-northern-ireland-1923|Public Records Act (Northern Ireland) 1923 (Department of Health NI)]]
What it means for AI use
UK approach to AI regulation: no general AI Act; sector regulators

The UK has no general AI statute. Existing law (data protection, equality, human rights, consumer, online safety, sector rules) applies to AI and is enforced by existing regulators. The King's Speech of 13 May 2026 contained no new primary AI legislation, though a Regulating for Growth Bill (AI sandboxes) and a Police Reform Bill (facial recognition framework) were announced. **Caveat:** Secondary source. A Private Member's Bill on artificial superintelligence (Alex Sobel MP) is due for second reading on 13 November 2026 and is unlikely to progress (Lewis Silkin, Sept 2026). Bill status not checked against the Parliament website.
[[https://www.resultsense.com/news/2026-05-28-uk-ai-regulatory-may-2026-roundup/|UK AI regulation: King's Speech, Crime Act and ICO converge in May (Resultsense)]]
ICO AI and biometrics strategy and 2026/27 AI commitments

The ICO regulates AI's use of personal data across the public and private sectors. It has committed to an AI code of practice, dedicated guidance on agentic AI and a new AI strategy with a 2026/27 workplan. Automated decision-making in public services and police facial recognition are among its priority areas. Public bodies should expect closer scrutiny of DPIAs and ADM safeguards. **Caveat:** Agentic AI guidance and the new AI strategy were not confirmed as published by 19 Oct 2026. The ADM and facial recognition priority areas come from secondary commentary.
[[https://ico.org.uk/about-the-ico/media-centre/news-and-blogs/2026/05/ico-response-to-government-on-safe-ai-powered-innovation/|ICO response to government on safe AI-powered innovation]]
EHRC: Artificial intelligence in public services

The equality regulator for Great Britain has published guidance on avoiding equality law breaches when public bodies use AI, and has monitored councils' AI use in England and Scotland. It enforces the PSED and the accessibility regulations in GB, so expect it to ask for evidence of equality analysis for AI systems. **Caveat:** Secondary report of a 2022 announcement; the outcomes of the monitoring were not retrieved.

[[https://www.localgovernmentlawyer.co.uk/community-safety/393-community-safety-news/51510-watchdog-to-monitor-how-public-bodies-use-ai-issues-guidance-on-avoiding-breaches-of-equality-law|Watchdog to monitor how public bodies use AI, issues guidance on avoiding breaches of equality law (Local Government Lawyer)]]
Equality Commission for Northern Ireland - Section 75 and accessibility enforcement

ECNI oversees public authorities' Section 75 equality schemes and enforces the public sector accessibility regulations in Northern Ireland. No AI-specific ECNI guidance was found, so NI bodies should apply ECNI's general screening and EQIA guidance to AI projects. **Caveat:** Searches of equalityni.org found no AI guidance; this is recorded as a gap.
[[https://www.gov.uk/guidance/public-sector-website-and-mobile-application-accessibility-monitoring|Public sector website and mobile application accessibility monitoring (names ECNI as NI enforcer)]]
CMA: Agentic AI and consumers / Complying with consumer law when using AI agents

Existing consumer law applies fully to AI agents. An organisation is responsible for its AI agent's breaches as it would be for an employee's, even if a third party supplies the system. Be transparent when people are dealing with an AI agent, build compliance in by design and keep human oversight. This is mainly relevant to public bodies that run trading or consumer-facing services. **Caveat:** Secondary summary dated 8 May 2026; the CMA's own publication date was not retrieved. How far it applies to public bodies depends on whether they act as traders.
[[https://www.cripps.co.uk/thinking/agentic-ai-and-consumers-cma-guidance/|Agentic AI and consumers: CMA guidance (Cripps summary)]]

Ofcom confirmed that generative AI chatbots and AI-generated content can fall under the Online Safety Act where users share content or where a tool searches multiple sites. Public bodies running public-facing chatbots that let users share content should check whether the Act's duties apply. **Caveat:** Most government chatbots are unlikely to be user-to-user services; check case by case. Online safety policy moved to DCMS in July 2026.

Government Security Classifications Policy (OFFICIAL, SECRET, TOP SECRET)

All HMG information is classified OFFICIAL, SECRET or TOP SECRET, with OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE a handling marking within OFFICIAL. AI tools must be assessed and approved by your organisation before OFFICIAL information goes into them; public consumer AI tools are not an approved route for sensitive or personal information. The policy itself does not contain AI-specific rules. **Caveat:** Last substantive update 5 Aug 2024 (Policy, Quick Read, Guidance 1.1 Working at OFFICIAL). The sentence on approval before use summarises departmental practice derived from the 2023 civil servant generative AI guidance, not this policy text. Devolved administrations use the classification scheme but its application to the wider public sector was not checked.
Guidance to civil servants on use of generative AI (2023)

The original rule for staff: never put sensitive information, personal data, classified material or information revealing unpublished government intent into publicly available generative AI tools, because government has no oversight of how that data is used. GOV.UK marks it superseded by the Generative AI Framework (and later the AI Playbook), but the principle still underpins departmental policies. **Caveat:** Status: marked 'superseded' on GOV.UK, not formally withdrawn (updated 29 Jan 2024). Kept for lineage.
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidance-to-civil-servants-on-use-of-generative-ai/guidance-to-civil-servants-on-use-of-generative-ai|Guidance to civil servants on use of generative AI]]
AI Playbook for the UK Government

Ten principles for using AI lawfully, securely and with human control across government, expanding the January 2024 Generative AI Framework for HMG. It covers data protection by design, security, transparency, auditability and buying AI, including asking suppliers for transparency and audit terms. It does not set explicit rules on which classification levels can go into which tools, so departmental policy fills that gap. **Caveat:** No explicit mention of OFFICIAL/OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, data residency, FOI or records of prompts was found when the HTML was read (in two parts). Not checked for a 2026 revision beyond the GOV.UK page date.
Cabinet Office (AI policy, post-July 2026); published by GDS
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government|Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government]]

Sets the expected security governance, risk management and protective security practice for government organisations, covering physical, personnel, cyber and information security. AI deployments sit inside it: they need an accountable owner, risk assessment and assurance like any other system. **Caveat:** Version 2.0; no newer version found on GOV.UK. Applicability to devolved administrations not confirmed.

Fourteen principles for assessing a cloud or SaaS service, including data in transit protection, asset protection and resilience, separation between customers, supply chain security and audit information. Use them to assess any AI service. Principle 2 asks you to understand which legislation your data is subject to, rather than requiring UK hosting. **Caveat:** Date is the 'reviewed' date for version 2.1.
[[https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/implementing-cloud-security-principles|Cloud security guidance — implementing the Cloud Security Principles (v2.1)]]
Guidelines for secure AI system development (NCSC)

Security practice across four lifecycle stages: secure design, development, deployment, and operation and maintenance, including threat modelling, supply chain, protecting models and logging. Teams building or integrating AI should use them alongside Secure by Design. **Caveat:** Version 1.0. International co-sealing partners not confirmed from the page read. Indexed with other AI security resources at https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/artificial-intelligence/ (updated 16 Sep 2026).
Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI

Thirteen baseline security principles across the AI lifecycle for developers, system operators and data custodians, with an implementation guide. It was submitted to ETSI as the basis of the international standard. Public bodies buying or building AI can use it as a supplier baseline. **Caveat:** Voluntary status not stated on the GOV.UK page itself. The promised update to mirror ETSI was not confirmed as published.
DCMS (listed publisher post-July 2026); originally published by DSIT (DSIT, abolished 21 July 2026; check the successor owner)
ETSI EN 304 223 — Baseline cyber security requirements for AI models and systems

The European Standard built from the UK AI Cyber Security Code of Practice (previously ETSI TS 104 223, with implementation report TR 104 128). It gives an internationally recognised reference that procurement can cite when asking AI suppliers for security assurance. **Caveat:** EN publication in December 2025 comes from techUK (Jan 2026) and EVS listing 'EN 304 223 V2.1.1 2025'; the ETSI page itself was not read. NCSC's May 2025 blog covers the TS version.
ETSI (standard); UK input from NCSC and DSIT (now DCMS) (DSIT, abolished 21 July 2026; check the successor owner)

[[https://www.techuk.org/resource/etsi-sets-out-new-european-standard-to-strengthen-ai-cyber-security.html|ETSI sets out new European standard to strengthen AI cyber security (techUK); NCSC blog on TS 104 223]]

The outcome-based framework government uses to assess critical systems (via GovAssure) and that NIS regulators use. Version 4.0 added sections on attacker methods, secure software development, stronger monitoring and threat hunting, and AI-specific cyber risks. AI services supporting critical government systems should be in scope of CAF assessment. **Caveat:** Release date and changes taken from Freevacy (grade B) summary of the NCSC release; the NCSC CAF page was not read directly.
[[https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/cyber-assessment-framework|NCSC releases Cyber Assessment Framework v4.0 (Freevacy summary)]]
GovAssure and the Government Cyber Action Plan

GovAssure assesses OFFICIAL government systems, including government-sector critical national infrastructure, against the CAF. The Government Cyber Action Plan (January 2026) sets objectives for securing public services. Departments should include significant AI services in their GovAssure scope where they are critical. **Caveat:** Action Plan published 6 Jan 2026 by DSIT; its CAF/GovAssure/AI content was not read in full. security.gov.uk page last updated 24 Sep 2026. The 'include AI services' sentence is a recommendation, not a quotation.
Government Cyber Unit (moved to DCMS in the July 2026 machinery of government change)
[[https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/govassure-for-central-government-departments/|GovAssure for central government departments (security.gov.uk); Government Cyber Action Plan (GOV.UK)]]
Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill

Would expand the NIS Regulations (including managed service providers and data centres), tighten incident reporting (initial notice within 24 hours, full report within 72 hours) and raise penalties. It has not received Royal Assent: as of 15 October 2026 it is at Lords Report stage. AI and cloud suppliers to essential services may come into scope. **Caveat:** Stage inferred from the bills page (HL Bill 49, 7 Sep 2026; page updated 15 Oct 2026). Reporting deadlines from BCLP (grade B). Scottish Government lodged a Legislative Consent Memorandum on 6 Jan 2026; consent outcome not confirmed.
DCMS (inferred post-July 2026; introduced by DSIT) (DSIT, abolished 21 July 2026; check the successor owner)
[[https://bills.parliament.uk/bills/4035|Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill — UK Parliament bills page]]
Scottish Government staff guidance on generative AI (FOI-released)

Scottish Government officials were told not to put sensitive information, policy details or anything they would not share with a member of the public into generative AI tools, to avoid hypothetical questions about policy, and to fact-check outputs. **Caveat:** Internal guidance released via FOI; date of the guidance and whether it is current are unconfirmed.

[[https://www.publictechnology.net/2025/05/15/science-technology-and-research/gen-ai-guidance-tells-scottish-officials-do-not-share-anything-you-would-not-share-with-a-member-of-the-public/|Gen AI guidance tells Scottish officials 'do not share anything you would not share with a member of the public' (PublicTechnology)]]
NICS Use of Generative AI Policy (Northern Ireland)

The Northern Ireland Civil Service adopted a Use of Generative AI Policy in June 2024; AI use is governed through existing data protection, security and ethics processes, and in The Executive Office the SIRO approves all AI use. **Caveat:** Not read from niassembly.gov.uk or finance-ni.gov.uk; the policy text itself was not found publicly.

What it means for AI use

Sets targets for central government departments and their agencies, including reporting the ICT and digital footprint and waste. The 2021-25 period has ended; HM Treasury's 2025-26 sustainability reporting guidance still aligns to its reporting requirements and refers to an 'upcoming 2025-30 commitment period'. **Caveat:** Marked historic on GOV.UK. The 2025-30 commitments were not found published at 19 Oct 2026 – unconfirmed. Original publication date not re-verified (page shows 15 Dec 2022 update).

Mandatory for UK central government annual reports: departments, agencies and NDPBs report ICT and digital waste by destination and footprint by device category. Data centre emissions count as Scope 1/2 if you own or control the data centre, otherwise Scope 3, and are 'material-only' reporting – so cloud-hosted AI compute is not a minimum reporting line. **Caveat:** No AI-specific content; last part of the page (about 12% of text) not read.
Greening Government: ICT and Digital Services Strategy 2020-2025 and successor

The 2020-25 strategy set five ICT sustainability objectives to March 2025; the 2024-25 annual report (July 2026) says most were on track. A UK government digital sustainability strategy led by Defra is promised but not published as at the latest sources, and Government Buying Standards are to gain ICT sustainability criteria. Until then there is no government-wide target for AI energy or water use. **Caveat:** Successor strategy status unconfirmed; Defra digital sustainability blog (26 March 2026) described it as upcoming. Neither source mentions AI energy or water.

[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/greening-government-ict-annual-report-2024-to-2025/greening-government-commitments-ict-annual-report-2024-to-2025|Greening Government Commitments ICT annual report 2024 to 2025]]
Using AI ethically and sustainably (draft AI Knowledge Hub guidance)

Draft civil-service guidance: first ask whether AI is needed at all, then choose the smallest model that can do the job, keep prompts short and avoid unnecessary back-and-forth. This is the clearest government steer towards routing work to cheaper, lower-energy models, which also reduces cost. **Caveat:** Seen only via a secondary report (XenoSpectrum, 29 Sept 2026) of a page on a 'dev' domain marked draft; not verified directly. Gives no measured energy or water figures.
Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, s.44 public bodies duties

Scottish public bodies must act in the way best calculated to help meet Scotland's emissions targets, help deliver the climate change adaptation programme, and act most sustainably. Annual reporting is required under the 2015 Order. Large AI and cloud contracts should therefore be appraised for emissions. **Caveat:** In force since 1 January 2011. The reporting Order (SSI 2015/347) and its later amendments were not re-checked.

Named Welsh public bodies have a well-being duty (s.3) to act in line with the sustainable development principle towards the seven well-being goals (s.4). AI investment decisions, including their long-term costs and environmental impacts, should be framed against these goals. **Caveat:** The Welsh public sector's 2030 net zero collective ambition and Net Zero Reporting Guide were seen only through a 2022 trade article – not verified.
What it means for AI use

The Government Legal Department's guide to the public law principles that decision-makers must follow: legality, rationality, procedural fairness and proper consideration. These apply equally when AI or automated tools support a decision, so officials must be able to explain and justify AI-assisted decisions and must not unlawfully fetter their discretion. **Caveat:** The landing page does not mention automated decision-making or AI; applying JOYS to AI is an interpretation. Scotland has a separate judicial review system; extent shown reflects the English courts focus and should be checked.
Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) - mandatory scope

Central government departments and arm's-length bodies that deliver public services or interact with the public must publish an ATRS record for algorithmic tools that significantly influence decisions with public effect or interact directly with the public, once the tool reaches beta, pilot or production. Retired tools need their record marked 'Retired'; FOI or data protection exemptions can justify marking fields 'EXEMPT'. **Caveat:** Policy, not statute. Page metadata shows an update on 9-10 September 2026 with no change note. Ownership after July 2026 not formally confirmed.
Government Digital Service (published under DSIT; GDS now in DCMS) (DSIT, abolished 21 July 2026; check the successor owner)

[[https://gov.uk/government/publications/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-mandatory-scope-and-exemptions-policy/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-atrs-mandatory-scope-and-exemptions-policy|Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: mandatory scope and exemptions policy]]
ATRS for the wider public sector (local government, devolved bodies)

Outside central government, ATRS is recommended but not required. It is endorsed by the Data Standards Authority, and the stated intent is to extend the requirement across the broader public sector over time. Councils and other bodies can publish records voluntarily. **Caveat:** No date has been set for extending the requirement. The MHCLG Local AI plans of July 2026 do not mention ATRS.
Government Digital Service / Data Standards Authority
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/algorithmic-transparency-recording-standard-hub|ATRS mandatory scope and exemptions policy; ATRS hub]]
Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 - automated decision-making (section 80, UK GDPR Articles 22A-22D)

From 5 February 2026, significant decisions based solely on automated processing can rely on a wider range of lawful bases, but safeguards are mandatory. People must be told about the decision and be able to make representations, get human intervention and contest it. Decisions based on special category data are restricted. The changes do not apply to decisions taken before 5 February 2026. **Caveat:** Commenced by SI 2026/82 (made 29 Jan 2026). The data subject complaints provisions (s.103) commenced 19 June 2026.
[[https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/82/made|The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/82)]]
ICO guidance on automated decision-making and profiling (DUAA update)

Draft ICO guidance explains when processing counts as solely automated decision-making with legal or similarly significant effects, and what safeguards are needed. Meaningful human involvement means an active review by someone with the authority and competence to change the outcome, before the decision is final, and it should be recorded. Public task is likely the relevant lawful basis for public bodies. **Caveat:** Consultation ran 31 March to 29 May 2026; final version not confirmed as published by 19 Oct 2026. The earlier version remains in use until the update is finalised.
ICO statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making

Regulations require the Information Commissioner to prepare a statutory code of practice on processing personal data when developing and using AI and automated decision-making. Once in force, courts and the ICO must take it into account, so public bodies deploying AI should expect it to become the main data protection benchmark. **Caveat:** Secondary commentary (Arnold & Porter) says the Regulations came into force on 12 May 2026 and the code is not expected to take effect until 2027; the made and in-force dates were not visible on the legislation page.
[[https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/425/contents/made|The Data Protection Act 2018 (Code of Practice on Artificial Intelligence and Automated Decision-Making) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/425)]]
Data and AI Ethics Framework and self-assessment tool

Teams designing, building, buying or running data and AI projects in the public sector should use this framework. It has seven principles: fairness, accountability and transparency, plus privacy, environmental sustainability, societal impact and safety, added in December 2025. Its self-assessment tool records decisions and trade-offs. **Caveat:** Retitled from 'Data Ethics Framework' on 18 December 2025; first published 2018.

This is a public register of AI systems used or developed by the Scottish Government and the wider Scottish public sector. Registration is mandatory for the Scottish Government and its core agencies; other public bodies are encouraged to register now, with mandatory registration planned in phases. Register any qualifying system and keep its lifecycle stage up to date. **Caveat:** Mandatory scope comes from a March/April 2024 announcement and a Data Lab case study (2026). The Digital Strategy delivery plan (Nov 2025) refers only to 'continued use' and does not state a mandate. No date has been found for extending the requirement beyond core Scottish Government. The register website could not be fetched.
Scottish Government (developed with the Scottish AI Alliance)
[[https://www.gov.uk/data-ethics-guidance/scottish-ai-register|Scottish AI Register (Data Ethics Guidance listing); Scottish AI Alliance 5-year case study]]
Public Law Project - Tracking Automated Government (TAG) register

A civil-society register of automated and algorithmic tools used by UK public bodies, compiled from FOI and other sources. It is not an official record, but it shows the outside scrutiny your tool may face and can help identify comparable systems and legal challenges. **Caveat:** Secondary, non-official source. Launch date and current coverage not verified in this check.
What it means for AI use
NAO: Use of artificial intelligence in government (2024)

The National Audit Office found 37% of 87 responding bodies had deployed AI (typically one or two use cases) and 70% were piloting or planning it. It said the draft AI adoption strategy lacked performance metrics, an implementation plan and clear ownership, and did not set out how benefits would be measured. Expect auditors to ask for baseline and benefits evidence. **Caveat:** Based on a 2023 survey; adoption has moved on since.
Public Accounts Committee: Use of AI in Government (HC 356)

The PAC's 18th report of 2024-26 (26 March 2025) followed the NAO work. Government's follow-up letter (18 November 2025) committed to consistent metrics for legacy technology costs and the cost of not acting, tracking remediation funding, and milestones and measures in the digital and AI roadmap – with deadlines moved into mid-2026. **Caveat:** Report conclusions not read in full; points taken from the government's November 2025 progress letter. Delivery status of the mid-2026 commitments unconfirmed.
House of Commons Public Accounts Committee
18th Report – Use of AI in Government
NAO: Good practice guide for organisations using AI

The NAO warns that AI productivity promises are 'not yet borne out by real world experience' – faster individual tasks do not automatically raise throughput where approvals and governance slow work. It asks for measurable objectives, clear pilot success criteria and committed funding, and flags dependence on large external suppliers and cloud providers. **Caveat:** Published May 2026 (exact day not shown). No cost framework and no environmental content.
[[https://www.nao.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/good-practice-guide-for-organisations-using-ai.pdf|Good practice guide for organisations using AI]]
NAO: Improving government's productivity through better cost information

Departments know total running costs but often lack activity-level cost information, so they cannot target expensive areas or prove productivity gains. The NAO recommends named senior owners for services and simple methods to measure staff time on activities – the baseline you need to show whether AI actually reduces cost per case. In February 2026 the Comptroller and Auditor General publicly questioned whether Copilot licences were delivering gains that justified their cost. **Caveat:** Copilot remark reported by a trade publication (11 Feb 2026), not an NAO report finding.
[[https://www.nao.org.uk/reports/improving-governments-productivity-through-better-cost-information/|Improving government's productivity through better cost information]]

About 20,000 staff in 12 organisations (including the Welsh Government) used M365 Copilot from September to December 2024. Users self-reported an average saving of 26 minutes a day; 17% saw no clear saving. The report includes no costs or return-on-investment analysis and could not say how saved time was used, so it cannot on its own justify licence spend. **Caveat:** Time savings are self-reported from range midpoints. DWP's separate Copilot trial evaluation (29 Jan 2026) exists, but its methods and figures were not read.
Magenta Book: Guidance on the impact evaluation of AI interventions

HM Treasury and Evaluation Task Force guidance: plan baselines and a comparison group before deploying AI, and strongly consider randomising access, timing or encouragement because AI is delivered digitally; otherwise use quasi-experimental designs. Its case study cautions against extrapolating early time savings to the whole civil service. **Caveat:** Last updated 15 May 2026; final part of the page not read.
[[https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-magenta-book/guidance-on-the-impact-evaluation-of-ai-interventions-html|Guidance on the Impact Evaluation of AI Interventions]]
What it means for AI use
One Big Thing 2025: AI for All

Every civil servant was asked to complete about one hour of foundational, responsible-use AI training (four 15-minute modules on Civil Service Learning) and take part in departmental activities. Check your department's One Big Thing hub for approved tools and local rules. **Caveat:** Participation by devolved civil services varies. Wales's Strategic AI Advisory Group discussed it in November 2025; Scottish Government and NICS participation was not confirmed.
[[https://moderncivilservice.blog.gov.uk/2025/10/14/one-big-thing-ai-for-all-is-live|One Big Thing: AI for All is live]]
Government Skills: Artificial intelligence skills for all

Free AI courses on Civil Service Learning at four levels: awareness (AI Fundamentals), working (ethics, business value, generative AI), practitioner (machine learning, NLP, working with LLMs) and a two-part Senior Civil Service pathway. Copilot learning is in the Digital skills for all curriculum.
Workforce Partnership Council: Managing technology that manages people / Using AI at work

Social partnership guidance agreed by the Welsh Government, public sector employers and trade unions. It requires human oversight of strategic decisions and human involvement in day-to-day decisions made by algorithmic management systems. It also calls for consultation and procurement due diligence, staff training, ongoing monitoring and protection of individual rights when AI is used to manage staff. **Caveat:** Guidance, not statute. It sits within the social partnership model, but its link to the duties in the Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023 was not confirmed.
Welsh Government Workforce Partnership Council (Welsh Government, unions, employers)
[[https://www.gov.wales/wales-public-sector-leading-way-responsible-ai-use|Wales' public sector leading the way in responsible AI use]]
Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act 2023

Sets up the Social Partnership Council and a social partnership duty requiring listed Welsh public bodies to seek consensus or compromise with recognised trade unions when setting well-being objectives and making decisions of a strategic nature. It also creates a socially responsible procurement duty. It is the statutory basis for involving unions in strategic AI workforce decisions in Wales. **Caveat:** The Act does not mention AI; applying it to AI is an interpretation. The summary of the duty is from general knowledge of the Act and was not re-read in section text during this check. Royal Assent date not shown on the contents page.
PCS demands for a civil service AI agreement

PCS, the largest civil service union, wants formal talks with the Cabinet Office on AI. Its demands include agreement before AI systems are introduced, disclosure of existing systems, no AI decisions about staff or AI monitoring of workers, no job losses, impact assessments before roll-out and shared productivity gains. Expect these points in departmental consultations on AI. **Caveat:** Union position, not an obligation.
[[https://www.pcs.org.uk/news-events/news/pcs-calls-formal-talks-cabinet-office-ai|PCS calls for formal talks with Cabinet Office on AI]]
FDA and Fabian Society: Adopt, Innovate, Transform

The senior civil servants' union and the Fabian Society call for an AI vision developed with staff and unions, better access to AI tools, and AI career paths and reward. They also want AI protections agreed with unions, including ways for staff to give feedback on how AI is used. **Caveat:** Union and think-tank position, not an obligation.
[[https://www.fda.org.uk/?p=9742|FDA and Fabian Society launch new AI report]]
TUC Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill campaign

The TUC has drafted a 'ready to go' AI bill that would require workers to be told when AI makes important decisions about them, give a right to an explanation and keep decisions human-centred. It has no legal force, but it frames union expectations for AI used in HR, pay, discipline and monitoring. **Caveat:** Campaign document. Page last modified 11 Nov 2025. No government bill has adopted it.
[[https://www.tuc.org.uk/node/529874|Launching the TUC's 'Ready to Go' AI Bill]]
